question: A 2-year-old has a 3-day history of sudden-onset cough after eating. The initial CXR is reported as 'normal'. Which of the following findings on an expiratory or lateral decubitus CXR would most support a diagnosis of foreign body aspiration?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are features of viral bronchiolitis or primary tuberculosis, not air-trapping from foreign body aspiration.

answers.text: Unilateral hyperinflation persisting on the expiratory film (obstructive emphysema)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ball-valve obstruction by a foreign body traps air distal to the obstruction. On expiration the affected side remains hyperinflated while the contralateral lung deflates normally — the key indirect sign.
Bilateral ground-glass suggests pulmonary oedema, viral pneumonitis, or aspiration pneumonitis — not the focal air-trapping expected with a central or lobar foreign body.
A paratracheal opacity suggests a mediastinal mass or lymph node, not a bronchial foreign body with air-trapping.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the ball-valve mechanism: a foreign body in a bronchus allows air in during inspiration but not out during expiration, causing the affected segment to remain overinflated on an expiratory film.
Well done. Unilateral obstructive emphysema — hyperinflation persisting on expiration — is the most reliable indirect CXR sign of foreign body aspiration.
